title: Pathophysiology: Inflammation, Fever & Tissue Repair—Protection, Injury and Healing
html:
Inflammation is a coordinated protective response to infection, tissue injury, ischemia, toxins, immune reactions, and other danger signals. It brings plasma proteins and leukocytes to the affected area, contains or removes the cause, clears damaged tissue, and begins repair. The same response can become harmful when excessive, prolonged, systemic, or directed against the body’s own tissues.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish inflammation from infection and immune activation.
  • Explain vascular change, leukocyte recruitment, mediators, and the cardinal local signs.
  • Compare acute and chronic inflammation.
  • Differentiate fever from hyperthermia and connect temperature change with assessment findings.
  • Interpret white blood cell patterns, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate as contextual cues.
  • Describe hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and remodeling in tissue repair.
  • Recognize local or systemic inflammatory patterns requiring urgent escalation.

Inflammation is not the same as infection

Infection is invasion and multiplication of a microorganism in the host. Inflammation is the host response to injury or danger. Infection commonly causes inflammation, but sterile trauma, infarction, burns, crystals, allergens, and autoimmune disease can also activate it. Conversely, an immunocompromised client may have a serious infection with a muted inflammatory response.

Do not treat redness or fever as a diagnosis
Identify the trigger, location, timing, host factors, exposures, procedures, devices, medications, and associated findings. Inflammation explains the response; it does not by itself determine whether the cause is bacterial, viral, traumatic, ischemic, allergic, autoimmune, or another process.

Danger recognition starts the response

Tissue-resident macrophages, mast cells, dendritic cells, and other sentinel cells recognize molecules from microbes and damaged cells. They release mediators such as histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, cytokines, and chemokines. Complement, coagulation, and kinin systems can amplify the response.

Mediators have different timing and effects. Histamine promotes rapid vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. Prostaglandins contribute to pain and fever. Cytokines such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor coordinate local and systemic responses. The benefit is recruitment and containment; the cost can include edema, pain, tissue injury, hypotension, or organ dysfunction when the response becomes excessive.

Vascular changes create the cardinal signs

Brief vasoconstriction may occur immediately after injury, followed by arteriolar vasodilation and increased local blood flow. This produces warmth and visible color change. Endothelial gaps and altered permeability allow protein-rich fluid to enter tissue, producing swelling. Chemical mediators, tissue pressure, and direct nerve stimulation contribute to pain. Loss of function results from pain, swelling, and tissue damage.

The classic local signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired function, but appearance varies with skin tone, depth, tissue type, perfusion, medications, and immune status. Compare with adjacent tissue and assess temperature, tenderness, edema, firmness, drainage, sensation, and function rather than relying on redness alone.

Leukocytes travel from blood to tissue

Slower blood flow and endothelial activation bring leukocytes toward the vessel wall. They roll, adhere, pass between endothelial cells, and follow chemotactic signals into tissue. Neutrophils often predominate early in acute bacterial inflammation and phagocytose microbes and debris. Monocytes enter tissue and mature into macrophages, which continue phagocytosis and coordinate both inflammation and repair.

Leukocytes release enzymes, reactive oxygen species, cytokines, and other substances that kill pathogens and remove damaged tissue. These tools can also injure nearby viable tissue. Resolution requires removal of the trigger, controlled mediator activity, clearance of inflammatory cells and debris, and restoration or replacement of tissue.

Acute inflammation has several possible outcomes

Acute inflammation develops rapidly and usually lasts a relatively short time. It may completely resolve, form an abscess or purulent collection, progress to chronic inflammation, or heal through fibrosis and scar formation. Outcome depends on the cause, duration, tissue’s regenerative capacity, extent of damage, blood supply, and host factors.

Fluid and cellular material leaving vessels form inflammatory exudate. Serous exudate is watery; fibrinous exudate is rich in fibrin; purulent exudate contains neutrophils, debris, and often microorganisms. Appearance can inform assessment but does not identify a pathogen or determine treatment without appropriate clinical and laboratory evaluation.

Chronic inflammation combines injury and repair

Chronic inflammation persists when the trigger cannot be eliminated, exposure continues, immune regulation is abnormal, or acute inflammation does not resolve. Macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells become more prominent. Ongoing cytokine release and tissue destruction occur alongside angiogenesis, fibroblast activation, and fibrosis.

Examples include persistent infection, autoimmune disease, prolonged foreign-body reaction, chronic toxin exposure, and metabolic inflammation. The client may have subtle systemic symptoms rather than dramatic local findings. Monitor function, nutrition, fatigue, anemia pattern, organ-specific complications, and treatment adverse effects over time.

Local defense can become a systemic response

Cytokines stimulate the liver to produce acute-phase proteins, alter leukocyte production, change metabolism, and act on the brain. Expected systemic findings may include fever, malaise, fatigue, reduced appetite, increased heart rate, and changes in the white blood cell count. These responses conserve resources and support defense, but they also increase oxygen and metabolic demand.

A systemic inflammatory pattern with hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status, oliguria, mottling, rising oxygen need, or other organ dysfunction is not a routine fever. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, perfusion, and neurologic status; activate the appropriate emergency or sepsis pathway according to policy. Older adults and immunocompromised clients may deteriorate without marked fever or leukocytosis.

Fever resets the temperature set point

Microbial products and inflammatory cytokines promote prostaglandin production in the hypothalamus, raising the regulated temperature set point. During the rising phase, the body now perceives its current temperature as too low, causing vasoconstriction, chills, shivering, and heat-seeking behavior. When the set point returns toward baseline, vasodilation and sweating promote heat loss.

Hyperthermia differs: body temperature rises without an upward reset of the hypothalamic set point because heat production or exposure exceeds heat loss. Heat stroke and certain medication reactions can cause dangerous hyperthermia and require immediate cooling and emergency management. Antipyretics lower a prostaglandin-mediated fever set point but do not correct uncontrolled environmental or metabolic heat production.

Assess temperature route and technique, age, baseline, environment, medications, neurologic status, hydration, oxygen demand, immune status, and associated symptoms. Do not assume every postoperative fever is infection, and do not dismiss fever without investigating the clinical pattern.

Inflammatory markers are nonspecific

The white blood cell count and differential can support interpretation, but a normal count does not exclude infection and an elevated count may reflect inflammation, stress, medication, tissue necrosis, or malignancy. Neutrophilia may accompany acute bacterial inflammation or physiologic stress; lymphocyte patterns vary with viral and immune processes; eosinophilia may occur with allergy, drug reaction, or parasitic disease.

C-reactive protein rises relatively quickly in response to cytokine signaling, while erythrocyte sedimentation rate often changes more slowly and is influenced by anemia, age, pregnancy, and plasma proteins. Neither test identifies a cause. Trends may help evaluate inflammatory activity when interpreted with symptoms, examination, cultures, imaging, other tests, and treatment timing.

Tissue repair uses four overlapping phases

Hemostasis begins immediately with vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and fibrin clot formation. Inflammation brings neutrophils and macrophages to clear microbes and devitalized tissue. Proliferation creates granulation tissue through angiogenesis and fibroblast activity, deposits collagen, contracts the wound, and restores the epithelial surface. Remodeling reorganizes collagen and strengthens the scar over weeks to months.

These phases overlap rather than follow rigid calendar boundaries. Regeneration restores the original cell type when viable cells and extracellular framework remain. Fibrosis replaces lost tissue with scar when damage is extensive or regeneration is limited. Scar tissue generally does not regain the full strength or specialized function of the original tissue.

Primary, secondary, and delayed closure

Wounds with closely approximated clean edges heal by primary intention with less granulation tissue and smaller scar. Wounds left open because of tissue loss or contamination heal by secondary intention with more granulation, contraction, and scarring. Delayed primary closure allows an initially open wound to be closed after contamination or swelling is controlled. Closure method follows the clinical plan; nurses do not independently close a concerning wound.

Factors that delay healing

Local problems include infection, poor perfusion, repeated pressure or shear, foreign material, edema, desiccation or excessive moisture, dead space, and mechanical stress. Systemic factors include diabetes, inadequate protein or micronutrients, dehydration, anemia or hypoxemia, tobacco exposure, advanced age, immune suppression, corticosteroids and other medications, vascular disease, and severe illness.

Assess the whole client and the wound trend. Support perfusion, pressure relief, mobility, glucose management, nutrition, hydration, infection prevention, and prescribed wound care. Escalate spreading warmth or discoloration, increasing pain, purulent drainage, odor after cleansing, dehiscence, necrosis, crepitus, fever with systemic change, or failure to progress.

Translate inflammation into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize: Locate the change and identify onset, trigger, local signs, systemic symptoms, host risks, and current therapy.
  2. Analyze: Decide whether findings fit an expected local response, infection, allergy, ischemia, autoimmune process, medication reaction, or systemic deterioration.
  3. Prioritize: Airway swelling, respiratory distress, shock, rapidly spreading tissue injury, severe pain out of proportion, and organ dysfunction outrank routine comfort measures.
  4. Act: Protect the client, obtain ordered specimens before antimicrobials when feasible without delaying emergency treatment, implement prescribed therapy, and communicate the cue cluster.
  5. Evaluate: Trend symptoms, temperature, perfusion, function, wound findings, output, laboratory markers, and adverse effects.

Clinical example

Two days after surgery, a client has incisional warmth and mild tenderness. These may occur during early healing, but the RN does not stop at that explanation. The client also has rapidly increasing pain, spreading firmness, tachypnea, new confusion, and falling urine output. The systemic cluster exceeds an expected local inflammatory response. The RN assesses stability, activates the urgent pathway, reports the trend and risk factors, implements prescribed actions, and repeatedly evaluates perfusion and organ function.
